Why I made this

I'm Nick, a registered nurse. I got my MSN at Johns Hopkins and have worked inpatient psych at Johns Hopkins Hospital and in the Bay Area.

It's practice for what a real assignment feels like: report from a tired night nurse, more patients than time, a phone that keeps buzzing, and one patient who is sicker than they look. The patients are made up. The situations are the ones that actually go wrong on a unit.

Most of the work is a series of small decisions: check this before that dose, see this patient first, say this on the phone. So that's how The Shift starts. Practice the decisions on their own until they're automatic, then put them together on a full shift.

It's in beta. If something is clinically off, every decision in the debrief has a link to tell me, and I read all of them.

Four drills, about a hundred patients

Each round is a few patients and a few minutes. Get one wrong and you see what happened to them, why, and one line worth remembering. Missed cards come back until you get them.

Med Pass 40 cards

Before the dose, what do you check? The number comes back. Then give, hold or call. Beta blockers, insulin, heparin, lithium, magnesium, blood.

Who's First 26 sets

Four patients, one nurse. Pick who you see first. Sepsis hiding as confusion, a quiet chest, a calm that isn't recovery.

SBAR 16 calls

Build the call line by line. Lead with your worry, give the background that matters, ask for what they need, read back the order.

De-escalation 16 scenarios

Every line you choose moves the agitation meter and the patient's face. Waiting rooms, psych holds, dementia, withdrawal, a doctor yelling in the hall.

  1. Play a daily round. One of each drill, five patients, about three minutes.
  2. Fix what you missed. Retry the ones you got wrong right away, or let them come back later.
  3. Then work a shift. Put it all together on a whole unit, from report to debrief.
Play today's round

Then put it together: a full shift

Four or five patients until handoff, about twenty minutes. A Next card always shows what to do next and walks you there. The clock only moves when you act. Every assessment, med pass and phone call costs minutes, and your other patients keep changing while you're busy.

06:58Report

Take report

The off-going nurse talks through every patient. Flag what matters onto your brain sheet. Some of what you hear is noise.

07:15Prioritize

Decide who's first

Rank your patients before you move. Nova, the charge nurse, compares your order with hers and tells you why at the end.

07:20to the end of shift

Work the hall

Assess, give or hold meds, delegate to your aide, talk with patients and families, and call the provider with SBAR. Look around the room; the clues are in it.

AfterDebrief

See what happened

An outcome for every patient, the decision that mattered most, and each call you made with the reasoning behind it, scored by skill and by NCLEX clinical judgment step.

What it practices

The clinical judgment the Next Generation NCLEX tests: noticing cues, prioritizing, acting, and checking whether it worked.

  • You choose what to look at. In a drill you pick what to check before you decide. In a shift there are no questions at all: you decide what to assess, in what order, and what to do about it.
  • Mistakes play out. Give the wrong med and the patient reacts. Hold the right one and the debrief explains why it mattered.
  • The traps are real ones. An order that's active but unsafe. A helpful family member. A report that says "probably a stomach bug."
  • A charge nurse who helps a little. Nova gives a few hints a shift. She'll point you somewhere; she won't do it for you.

Play a round, then tell me what broke.
